title: Architecture of India
wiki_lead:
Indian architecture is rooted in the history, culture, and religion of India. Among multiple architectural styles and traditions, the best-known include the many built in accordance to Indian religion and philosophy with Hindu, Jain, Buddhist, and Sikh styles of architecture being the most prevalent in India, with Indo-Islamic architecture, Rajput architecture, Mughal architecture, South Indian architecture, and Indo-Saracenic architecture having a strong presence as well.
Early Indian architecture was made from wood, which did not survive due to rotting and instability in the structures. Instead, the earliest surviving examples of Indian architecture are Indian rock-cut architecture, including many Buddhist, Hindu, and Jain temples.
Hindu temple architecture is traditionally divided into two main architectural styles: the Dravidian style of southern India and Nagara style of northern India, with several regional variations that combine elements of both. Other regional styles, such as the Vesara style of the Deccan plateau and the Kalinga style of eastern India, developed through local tastes. In addition to temple architecture, domestic housing styles in India also vary widely between regions, reflecting differences in climate, geography, building materials, and cultural traditions. 
The first major Islamic empire in India was the Delhi Sultanate, which led to the development of Indo-Islamic architecture, combining Indian and Islamic architectural features. The rule of the Mughal Empire, when Mughal architecture evolved, is regarded as the zenith of Indo-Islamic architecture, with the Taj Mahal being the high point of their contribution. Indo-Islamic architecture got influenced by existing indigenous Hindu elements of style and later fused with Rajput and Sikh architecture as well.
During the British colonial period, European styles including Neoclassical, Gothic Revival, and Baroque became prevalent across India. The amalgamation of Indo-Islamic and European styles led to a new style, known as the Indo-Saracenic style. Following the events succeeding India's independence from Britain, new European modernist ideas spread amongst Indian architects as a means of progressing as a new republic. Swiss-French architect Le Corbusier was commissioned by the Indian government to design the city of Chandigarh, which influenced a generation of architects towards modernism in the 20th century. The continued economic reforms further bolstered modern architecture and the urban layout of India, as the country became more integrated with the world's economy.

Neolithic period
In South India, the Neolithic period began in 6500 BCE and lasted till around 1400 BCE when the Megalithic transition period began. The South Indian Neolithic period is characterized by ash mounds from 2500 BCE in the region of Karnataka, which later expanded into Tamil Nadu.

Neolithic settlements have been found in many parts of India. The earliest clear evidence of the megalithic urn burials, discovered at various places in Tamil Nadu, date back to 1000 BCE. The most notable megalithic urn was discovered in Adichanallur, 24 kilometres (15 mi) from Tirunelveli, where archaeologists from the Archaeological Survey of India unearthed 12 urns containing human skulls, skeletons and bones, husks, grains of charred rice and Neolithic celts, confirming the presence of the Neolithic period 2800 years ago.

grok_lead: The architecture of India represents a profound synthesis of indigenous traditions, regional variations, and external influences spanning over 5,000 years, from the planned urban layouts of the Indus Valley Civilization to contemporary sustainable designs, characterized by intricate craftsmanship, symbolic religious elements, and adaptive engineering in diverse climates. Ancient Indian architecture originated with the Indus Valley Civilization (c. 3300â1300 BCE), featuring advanced urban planning in cities like Mohenjo-Daro and Harappa, including grid layouts, sophisticated drainage systems, and monumental structures such as the Great Bath, which demonstrated early mastery of brickwork and water management. During the Vedic and Mauryan periods (c. 1500â185 BCE), architecture shifted toward wooden structures and rock-cut caves, with Emperor Ashoka's polished sandstone pillars and stupas like those at Sanchi exemplifying Buddhist influences through symbolic domes and railings carved with narrative reliefs. The Gupta Empire (c. 320â550 CE) marked the emergence of structural stone temples, such as the Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh (c. 5th century CE), introducing proto-shikhara towers and symbolic iconography that laid foundations for later Hindu styles. Medieval Indian architecture diversified into distinct regional temple styles under Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist patronage: the Nagara style in northern India, with its towering shikharas and mandapas as seen in the Kandariya Mahadeva Temple at Khajuraho (c. 1030 CE); the Dravida style in the south, featuring stepped gopurams and vimanas like those at the Brihadeeswarar Temple in Thanjavur (c. 1010 CE), built by the Chola dynasty using massive granite blocks; and the hybrid Vesara style in the Deccan, blending elements in structures like the Hoysaleswara Temple at Halebidu. The advent of Islamic rule from the 12th century introduced Persian and Central Asian elements, such as arches, domes, and minarets, evident in the Delhi Sultanate's Qutb Minar (c. 1199 CE), the tallest brick minaret in the world, and the Alai Darwaza gateway, which fused Indo-Islamic motifs with local trabeate construction. The Mughal era (1526â1857 CE) elevated this synthesis to imperial grandeur, with symmetrical gardens, iwans, and white marble inlays, most iconically in the Taj Mahal (1632â1653 CE) in Agra, commissioned by Shah Jahan as a mausoleum blending Persian paradise gardens with Hindu chhatris and jali screens. Mughal forts like the Red Fort in Delhi (1639â1648 CE) further showcased red sandstone jaali work and pavilions reflecting both power and aesthetics. Colonial architecture from the 18th to 20th centuries incorporated European neoclassical, Gothic Revival, and Indo-Saracenic styles, as in the Victoria Memorial in Kolkata (1906â1921 CE), which combined Mughal domes with British baroque elements to symbolize imperial authority. Post-independence ( 1947 onward), modern Indian architecture embraced international modernism tempered by context, exemplified by Le Corbusier's planned city of Chandigarh (1950s) with its Brutalist capitol complex, while contemporary practices focus on sustainability, as in Charles Correa's Kanchanjunga Apartments (1987) integrating climate-responsive features like stepped profiles for ventilation. Overall, Indian architecture's enduring legacy lies in its adaptability, from seismic-resistant temple designs to eco-friendly urbanism, influencing global practices through motifs like the lotus dome and fractal geometry in patterns.
